item.title: Physical consistency and completeness in the data-driven modeling of microwave absorbing materials
item.description:
Machine learning (ML) has been applied to the modeling of microwave absorbing materials, including the prediction of electromagnetic parameters and reflection loss (RL), yet the physical consistency of such models is rarely examined. This paper addresses two types of physical consistency problems in data-driven modeling: the physical inconsistency of predicted outputs and the physical incompleteness of input features. On the output side, we constructed a numerical integrator based on the Kramers-Kronig (KK) relation to test permittivity spectra output by ML models. The results show that none of the four examined spectra from three studies satisfied the KK relation, indicating that the model outputs markedly violate physical consistency. On the input side, we took a published MXene study as a case example. There is no thickness, which determines the RL jointly with other variables, in its feature space. Using physically consistent synthetic data, we conducted controlled experiments under two data settings and two partition schemes. It was found that without the thickness, the model captured only a limited part of the RL variance and could not distinguish the labels corresponding to different thicknesses. Adding the thickness restored the performance, with the R2 rising from 0.364 to 0.956 under the fullthickness setting. Finally, we further discussed three approaches to embedding the KK constraint into the modeling workflow. Our results suggest that physical consistency and completeness are necessary conditions for building reliable data-driven models, and that global integral constraints such as the KK relation cannot be learned implicitly from small samples.

Hongtao Zeng

item.title: Metal-Free Spin Crossover Through Nitrogen-Intercalated Graphene Under Pressure
item.description:
Spin crossover (SCO) phenomena, in which the spin state of an atom changes due to an external stimulus, have been the subject of ongoing research interest to this day. However, the considered atoms have been limited to transition metals like iron or cobalt. In this theoretical study, we show for the first time that external pressure can cause a nitrogen atom, i.e., a non-metal, to transit from a high spin (HS) to a low spin (LS) configuration. This nitrogen atom is located between two graphene sheets (N@Graphene) to mediate anisotropic pressure, serving as a proof-of-principle system on a periodic density functional theory (DFT) level. With increasing pressure, the distance between nitrogen and the graphene sheets decreases, leading to a SCO at a pressure below 5 GPa. To understand more about the mechanism behind the SCO, a finite model system, N@Circumcoronene, was constructed to allow the application of various electronic structure analysis tools for finite systems. These tools confirm that the SCO is the result of a closed-shell-dominated interaction in the sandwich structure. This work introduces a promising basis for the realization of a new class of materials with pressure-sensitive SCO involving main group atoms.

Nico Kißing, Mausumi Chattopadhyaya, Tim Neudecker

item.title: Tautomerism and Diradical Character: Chemical and Electronic Structure of a High-Performance Organic Electrode Material
item.description:
Bis-tetraaminobenzoquinone (TAQ) is a high-performance organic electrode material whose molecular structure remains a subject of debate, which we address in this joint experimentaltheoretical study. Using density functional theory (DFT) across multiple scales, from isolated molecules to periodic crystal structures, this work provides an atomistic insight into the structural and electronic complexity of TAQ. Our analysis reveals a rich tautomeric landscape, identifying two energetically competitive forms: the originally proposed piperazine tautomer and a proton-shifted variant featuring a pyrazine-based core and NH 3 groups at the periphery. Crucially, both tautomers exhibit near-degenerate closed-shell singlet, open-shell singlet (diradical character), and triplet states. We attribute the open-shell electronic character to resonance forms that contain quinoid-like and aromatic diradical motifs. The importance of open-shell states is confirmed by variable-temperature electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy, which detects a ∆m S = 2 transition and yields a singlet–triplet gap of only 0.4–0.7 meV. Constrained DFT configuration interaction (cDFT-CI) calculations demonstrate that this open-shell character can enhance efficient electron transfer. These findings resolve discrepancies in experimental NMR data, previously interpreted as evidence for the structurally related TAPT compound, by showing that they arise naturally from a tautomeric form of TAQ. This tautomer accounts for the elusive origin of the organic spin, which stems from its unique open-shell electronic structure.

Juliane Heitkämper, Sören Schlittenhardt, Alexander Tombrink, Sabine Richert, Birgit Esser, Birger Horstmann, Piotr de Silva, Juan Maria García-Lastra

item.title: Gain, Retention, or Loss of Aromaticity upon Surface Adsorption: π-Electron Systems on Cu(111)
item.description:
Understanding the interactions between metal surfaces and the π-electron systems of flat-lying polycyclic conjugated hydrocarbons is central to designing metal–organic interfaces and on-surface synthesis. This surface interaction is sometimes rationalized in terms of aromaticity, which is usually evaluated for gas phase model systems and rarely for adsorbed molecules. Here, we use density functional theory to study changes in geometric and electronic aromaticity for 22 π-electron systems upon adsorption on Cu(111), from physisorption to strong chemisorption. Surprisingly, the change in aromaticity does not simply follow the interaction strength. Instead, population of the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital causes two competing effects: bond length equalization, driven by the gas phase bond length alternation, and bond elongation, determined by the adsorption height. Consequently, physisorbed molecules retain their aromaticity, while chemisorbed molecules can gain, locally alter, or lose it. The change in aromaticity can be decomposed into a deformation contribution (structural change upon adsorption) and an interaction contribution (direct electronic effect of the surface). Geometric indices capture only the deformation contribution, which shows the same trends in the electronic indices. The interaction contribution is negligible for the critical-point-based index but lowers the bond-order-based aromaticity of all molecules. This reflects the overlap of molecular and surface electron densities rather than a loss of aromaticity. Thus, geometric aromaticity indices, which require only the adsorption structure, provide enough insights into the changes upon adsorption. The gas phase aromaticity is therefore only a partial guide, as aromaticity at interfaces is a property of the full molecule–surface system.

Jakob Schramm, Ralf Tonner-Zech

item.title: synthmc: a precedent-based synthesizability score for transition metal complexes
item.description:
Data-driven methods are increasingly being used for the in silico discovery of transition metal complexes (TMCs), ranging from machine learning models for high-throughput screening and generative models proposing new candidates to evolutionary algorithms for their de novo design. However, computationally discovered or designed TMCs are only rarely realized experimentally, in part because their synthesis is difficult and often not considered during the design process. At the same time, established synthetic accessibility scores for organic small molecules cannot be transferred to TMCs beyond their constituent ligands, as their fragment-based heuristics and molecular representations do not capture the influence of the metal center, coordination mode, and steric effects on coordinability. Here, we present synthmc, a precedent-based synthesizability score for TMCs that combines the precedent of ligands, coordination environments, and degrees of steric crowding in a reference corpus constructed from experimentally reported complexes in the Cambridge Structural Database. Evaluated on random and time-based validation sets, synthmc assigns, on average, lower scores to more recently reported complexes, consistent with their reduced precedent, indicating its ability to identify novel chemistry. We hope that synthmc will help to prioritize synthetically accessible candidates in high-throughput screening and generative design of TMCs and, more broadly, motivate the development of more comprehensive synthesizability assessments for TMCs, for example based on retrosynthetic approaches or expert evaluations.

Hannes Kneiding
